t.1.84.1: I am Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa and father of Pūru; because I held all beings in contempt, I have been cast down from the world of the gods, Siddhas and seers, and, fallen away, my merit spent, I am falling headlong.
t.1.84.2: For I am older in years than you; therefore I do not offer you a greeting of respect. Among the twice-born, he who is senior in learning, in austerity, or by birth is the one who is to be honored.
t.1.84.3: You said, O king, that he who is advanced in years is the elder, and so you did not greet us at all; yet it is the one who, being learned, is also advanced in years who alone is worthy of honor among the twice-born.
t.1.84.4: They declare that what runs counter to righteous deeds is evil, and in the one who is not inclined to virtue that evil abides, bringing a world of sin. The good do not follow this way of the wicked, for their own self speaks in accord with them.
t.1.84.6: Many are the various conditions in the world of the living, dependent on fate, in which effort and authority are lost. Whatever befalls him, the steadfast man should not be struck down, having understood with his own reason that destiny is stronger.
t.1.84.5: Vast and great indeed was my wealth, yet however much I strive, I shall not attain it again. He who, having reflected thus, lives devoted to the good of his own self, he understands while still living.
t.1.84.7: For whether a creature finds happiness or sorrow, it finds what is subject to fate, not what comes by its own power. Therefore, deeming destiny to be mighty, one should never be consumed with grief, nor ever be elated.
t.1.84.8: One should not be tormented by sorrow nor exult in happiness; the steadfast man should always conduct himself with evenness. Considering that fate is stronger, he should never be inflamed with distress, nor ever be elated.
t.1.84.10: Those born of sweat, those born from eggs, and those that sprout from the earth, creeping things, worms, and fishes in the water, as well as stones, grass, wood, and everything else, all return to their own original nature when their allotted time is exhausted.
t.1.84.9: Never am I bewildered by fear, Aṣṭaka, nor is there any anguish in my mind, for I reflect that as the Ordainer disposes me in the world, so surely shall I be.
t.1.84.12: Aṣṭaka said: O lord of kings, whatever chief worlds you have enjoyed, for what length of time and in what manner, tell me all of that truly, O king, for you speak of the laws like one who knows the field.
t.1.84.11: Having understood the impermanence of pleasure and pain, why should I, Aṣṭaka, give myself over to grief? What indeed could I do, and having done what would I not be tormented? Therefore, remaining vigilant, I shun grief.
t.1.84.13: I was a king here, sovereign over the whole earth; then I truly won great worlds. There I dwelt for a full thousand years, and then I came to the highest world.
t.1.84.14: Then I dwelt for a full thousand years in the lovely city of Puruhūta, which has a thousand gates and stretches a hundred yojanas; after that I have come to a higher world.
t.1.84.15: Then, having reached the divine, ageless world of Prajāpati, lord of the worlds, so hard to attain, I dwelt there for a full thousand years; after that I went on to the highest world.
t.1.84.16: Having conquered the worlds, I dwelt as I pleased in the abode of god after god, honored by all the Thirty, my might and splendor equal to those of the lords.
t.1.84.18: As I dwelt there, attached to the pleasures of the gods, after a great span of time had passed, a messenger of the gods, fierce of form, then cried out to me exceedingly loudly three times in a protracted voice, "Fall!"
t.1.84.17: Thus I dwelt in Nandana, assuming any form at will, for ten thousand hundreds of years, sporting with the Apsarases and gazing upon flowering trees of holy fragrance and lovely form.
t.1.84.19: This much is known to me, O lion among kings: then, my merit exhausted, I fell from Nandana, and in the sky I heard the voices of the gods, who grieved for me out of compassion, O lord of men.
t.1.84.20: "Alas, how grievous! Yayāti, his merit exhausted, is falling, he who did meritorious deeds and whose fame was pure!" Then, as I was falling, I said to them, "How might I fall into the midst of the virtuous?"
t.1.84.21: Your sacrificial ground was pointed out by them, and having seen it I have swiftly come here, gladdened, taking as my guide the scent of the oblations and the trailing smoke of the sacrificial ground.
